If [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(2)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(4)] are independent, and [MATH: Y=X_1+X_2], then calculate [MATH: P(Y<3).]
Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_2)], then

[MATH: X_1+X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).]

Because [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent variables, we have

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(2 + 4); ∼Po(6).]

The probability mass function of [MATH: Y\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)] is given by

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{\lambda^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots]

Here, [MATH: Y\sim \textrm{Po}(6)], so the probability distribution of [MATH: Y] is

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{6^y e^{-6}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots]

Therefore, [MATH: P(Y < 3)|= P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2); = (6^{0}e^{− 6})/(0!) + (6^{1}e^{− 6})/(1!) + (6^{2}e^{− 6})/(2!); ≈ 0.062.]

items.title: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sum of Poisson Random Variables in Context

sections.normalized_html: A popular mobile app has two download options, one for tablets and one for smartphones. Customers downloaded the app at an average rate of [MATH: 5] times per minute on tablets and [MATH: 6] times per minute on smartphones. Assuming that each download is mutually independent, find the probability that the app will be downloaded more than five times over the next minute.
sections.readable_text: A popular mobile app has two download options, one for tablets and one for smartphones. Customers downloaded the app at an average rate of [MATH: 5] times per minute on tablets and [MATH: 6] times per minute on smartphones. Assuming that each download is mutually independent, find the probability that the app will be downloaded more than five times over the next minute.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's define the following random variables:

  • Let [MATH: X_1] be the number of times the app is downloaded on tablets over the next minute.

  • Let [MATH: X_2] be the number of times the app is downloaded on smartphones over the next minute.

We assume that [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables.

  • The app is downloaded, on average, at a rate of [MATH: 5] times per minute on tablets. Thus, [MATH: X_1 \sim \textrm{Po}(5).]

  • The app is downloaded, on average, at a rate of [MATH: 6] times per minute on smartphones. Thus, [MATH: X_2 \sim \textrm{Po}(6).]

Let [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2.] We want to find [MATH: P(Y > 5).]

Since [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(5)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(6)] are independent Poisson random variables, then

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(5 + 6); ∼Po(11).]

So, the probability distribution of [MATH: Y] is

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{11^y e^{-11}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots\,.]

There are infinitely many values of [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: Y >5.] However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

[MATH: P(Y > 5)|= 1 − P(Y ≤ 5)]

Computing the complement, we get

[MATH: P(Y ≤ 5)|= P(Y ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}); = P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2); + P(Y = 3) + P(Y = 4) + P(Y = 5); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3) + f(4) + f(5); = (11^{0}e^{− 11})/(0!) + (11^{1}e^{− 11})/(1!) + (11^{2}e^{− 11})/(2!); + (11^{3}e^{− 11})/(3!) + (11^{4}e^{− 11})/(4!) + (11^{5}e^{− 11})/(5!); ≈ 0.0375.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(Y > 5)|= 1 − P(Y ≤ 5); ≈ 1 − 0.0375; = 0.9625.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The sum of two independent Poisson random variables is also a Poisson random variable.

Content:
More precisely, if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables such that [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_2)], then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).]

Content:
We'll prove this in a separate lesson.

Content:
For example, if [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}({\color{red}{4}})] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}({\color{blue}{5}})] are independent, then

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(4 + 5); ∼Po(9).]

Content:
There is some nice intuition behind this rule. For example, consider the following situation:

Content:
- the random variable [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}({\color{red}{4}})] represents the number of red buses that arrive at a bus station every hour, and
- the random variable [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}({\color{blue}{5}})] represents the number of blue buses that arrive the same bus station every hour.

Content:
Under this model, we assume that an average of [MATH: \color{red}{4}] red buses and [MATH: \color{blue}{5}] blue buses arrive at the bus station every hour.

Content:
Then, the random variable

Content:
[MATH: Y = X_1+X_2 \sim \textrm{Po}(9)]

Content:
represents the number of buses (both red and blue) that arrive at the bus station every hour, arriving at an average rate of [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}+{\color{blue}{5}} = 9] buses per hour.

Content:
Watch out! The discussion above only applies to sums. The difference of two independent Poisson random variables is not a Poisson random variable!

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Distribution of a Sum of Poisson Random Variables

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(4)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(2.3)] are independent, then what is the distribution of [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_2)], then

[MATH: X_1+X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).]

Because [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent variables, we have

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(4 + 2.3); ∼Po(6.3).]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sum of Poisson Random Variables

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(2)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(4)] are independent, and [MATH: Y=X_1+X_2], then calculate [MATH: P(Y<3).]
Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables, where [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_2)], then

[MATH: X_1+X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).]

Because [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent variables, we have

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(2 + 4); ∼Po(6).]

The probability mass function of [MATH: Y\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda)] is given by

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{\lambda^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots]

Here, [MATH: Y\sim \textrm{Po}(6)], so the probability distribution of [MATH: Y] is

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{6^y e^{-6}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots]

Therefore,
[MATH: P(Y < 3)|= P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2); = (6^{0}e^{− 6})/(0!) + (6^{1}e^{− 6})/(1!) + (6^{2}e^{− 6})/(2!); ≈ 0.062.]

Item 8 — Example: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sum of Poisson Random Variables in Context

Example Prompt:
A popular mobile app has two download options, one for tablets and one for smartphones. Customers downloaded the app at an average rate of [MATH: 5] times per minute on tablets and [MATH: 6] times per minute on smartphones. Assuming that each download is mutually independent, find the probability that the app will be downloaded more than five times over the next minute.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's define the following random variables:

- Let [MATH: X_1] be the number of times the app is downloaded on tablets over the next minute.
- Let [MATH: X_2] be the number of times the app is downloaded on smartphones over the next minute.

We assume that [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent Poisson random variables.

- The app is downloaded, on average, at a rate of [MATH: 5] times per minute on tablets. Thus, [MATH: X_1 \sim \textrm{Po}(5).]
- The app is downloaded, on average, at a rate of [MATH: 6] times per minute on smartphones. Thus, [MATH: X_2 \sim \textrm{Po}(6).]

Let [MATH: Y = X_1+X_2.] We want to find [MATH: P(Y > 5).]

Since [MATH: X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(5)] and [MATH: X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(6)] are independent Poisson random variables, then

[MATH: Y = X_{1} + X_{2}|∼Po(5 + 6); ∼Po(11).]

So, the probability distribution of [MATH: Y] is

[MATH: f(y) = \dfrac{11^y e^{-11}}{y!}, \qquad y=0,1,2,\ldots\,.]

There are infinitely many values of [MATH: Y] such that [MATH: Y >5.] However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

[MATH: P(Y > 5)|= 1 − P(Y ≤ 5)]

Computing the complement, we get

[MATH: P(Y ≤ 5)|= P(Y ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}); = P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1) + P(Y = 2); + P(Y = 3) + P(Y = 4) + P(Y = 5); = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3) + f(4) + f(5); = (11^{0}e^{− 11})/(0!) + (11^{1}e^{− 11})/(1!) + (11^{2}e^{− 11})/(2!); + (11^{3}e^{− 11})/(3!) + (11^{4}e^{− 11})/(4!) + (11^{5}e^{− 11})/(5!); ≈ 0.0375.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(Y > 5)|= 1 − P(Y ≤ 5); ≈ 1 − 0.0375; = 0.9625.]
